SUBSECTION.NAME: Functions with Local Variables
SUBSECTION.TEXT:
To handle functions with local variables, we extend the environment model in a straightforward manner. Consider for example the function f_3 from section and its helper function square.
f_3_b f_3_b_example 456
def square(z): return z * z def f_3(x, y): a = 1 + x * y b = 1 - y return x * square(a) + y * b + a * b
f_3_b_example
print(f_4(3, 4))
As with simple functions, a call f_3(3, 4) creates a new environment, E1, beginning with a frame in which x and y, the parameters of f_3, are bound to the arguments 3 and 4, respectively. However, f_3 has declaration assignments for the local variables a and b, and subsequent references to the local variables need to refer to their values. To prepare for the evaluation of declaration assignments and their variables, the frame has bindings for a and b in addition to x and y. Before the the body of f_3 is evaluated, a and b do not refer to any values yet, we say they are unassigned. The evaluation of the assignments to a and b follows the rule for assignment in the previous section and thus modifies the frame so that a refers to 13, the result of evaluating 1 + x * y, and b refers to -3, the result of evaluating 1 - y. The remaining statement in the function body, return x * square(a) + y * b + a * b, contains the call square(a), which evaluates the body of square, return z * z, in a new environment, E2, beginning with a frame in which the parameter z refers to 13. The evaluation of the return expression of f_3 uses the result 169 and the values of the other variables in the environment E1 and computes 456 as the result of the function call f_3(3, 4). When the
set! reassignment
is executed, the binding of balance in E1 is changed. At the completion of the call to W1, balance is 50, and the frame that contains balance is still pointed to by the
procedure function
object W1. The frame that binds amount (in which we executed the code that changed balance) is no longer relevant, since the
procedure function
call that constructed it has terminated, and there are no pointers to that frame from other parts of the environment. The next time W1 is called, this will build a new frame that binds amount and whose enclosing environment is E1. We see that E1 serves as the place that holds the local state variable for the

expression in the body of make-withdrawmake_withdraw.Whether W1 and W2 share the same physical code stored in the computer, or whether they each keep a copy of the code, is a detail of the implementation. For the interpreter we implement in chapter, the code is in fact shared. We see here why W1 and W2 behave as independent objects. Calls to W1 reference the state variable balance stored in E1, whereas calls to W2 reference the balance stored in E2. Thus, changes to the local state of one object do not affect the other object.
